Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 67
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 48

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Shouting: Shouting, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Auditory (Loud Noises): Loud noises
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Work or Study: Going to work or study, Positive Reframing: I force myself to think only positive thoughts, Overeat: eat excessively to manage distress
  Threat: Threat in Delays: When something takes longer than expected I assume something bad is happening, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now.
  Negative Appraisals: Self-Comparison: Somebody else would not have gotten into this situation, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place

Vignette:
Martin Keller is a 67-year-old White American man who has spent most of his adult life in schools, and for the past several years has served as a principal. He came to treatment after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that he still struggles to describe out loud. When he tries, his words thin out and then stop; he says he can see it perfectly, but he cannot seem to put it into language in a way that feels complete. What remains most available to him is not a tidy story but a sequence of images that returns like a film: the sudden movement of another car, the violent instant of impact, shattered sound, and the unmistakable conviction that he might die there in the vehicle. Even now, when the memory comes, it does not feel like something that happened in the past. For brief moments he feels as if he is back inside the collision, braced in his seat and waiting for the next hit.

In the months afterward, Martin found that the world no longer felt ordinary or basically safe to him. He had come to believe that danger was everywhere and that the collision had changed him in a permanent way. He compared himself harshly to an imagined steadier person, telling himself that somebody else would not have gotten into that situation, somebody else would have handled things better. He speaks about himself now with a note of disappointment, as though the accident exposed a weakness he cannot forgive. What frightens him almost as much as the memory itself is the sense that he is no longer the man he was before, that something in him has been altered for the worse and is not likely to return.

Because he works as a school principal, his daily environment repeatedly confronts him with things that set his body on edge. Raised voices in hallways, a teacher calling sharply across a cafeteria, students shouting during a conflict on school grounds—these moments can jolt him instantly. Loud noises have a similar effect: a slammed door, metal chairs scraping hard across the floor, the sudden blast of a microphone at an assembly. He also reacts strongly to visual reminders of crashes. A damaged car on the roadside, footage of a traffic accident on a local news segment, even the sight of two vehicles stopped close together after a minor fender-bender can pull him back into the collision with unnerving speed. In those moments he does not simply remember; he feels seized by it.

At work, he has increasingly tried to limit his exposure to the setting altogether. He has begun avoiding going in when he can, delegating in-person matters he once would have handled himself and lingering at home before leaving for school. The building that used to feel familiar now feels unpredictable to him because anything loud or sudden might happen around the next corner. This has had visible consequences. Staff have noticed that he is less present, slower to walk into tense situations, less available in the spontaneous way principals often need to be. At home, too, the strain has accumulated. Martin has trouble falling asleep and often cannot stay asleep, lying awake with his body feeling watchful long after he knows intellectually that he is in his own bedroom and safe. He says he cannot relax, even in quiet moments with his wife, and if something is delayed—a family member running late, a call not returned when expected, traffic holding someone up—his mind quickly jumps to the assumption that something bad has happened.

Martin has developed ways of trying to manage this, though they have not brought much relief. He pushes himself to think only positive thoughts, almost as a rule: don’t dwell on it, look on the bright side, be grateful it wasn’t worse. He describes this effort with the disciplined tone of someone used to holding himself together for other people. But the memories return anyway, cutting across his attempts at forced optimism. He has also found himself eating excessively when distressed, particularly in the evening after difficult days, using food to settle himself when his nerves feel too activated to bear.

By the time he sought help, Martin was exhausted by how narrow his life had become and by the effort required to appear composed at school and at home. What finally pushed him into treatment was not one single dramatic incident but the accumulation of them: another sleepless stretch, another day avoiding work, another moment of feeling hijacked by shouting in the school hallways. He wants, very simply, to feel present in his own life again. At the same time, he is afraid that the collision has marked him permanently, that this constant readiness for disaster is now who he is.
